standard: Aircraft registers don't agree on a format. I got them into one feed.
evidence: Each register becomes a SQLite artifact, and a private Cloud Run service handles the lookups and attaches the source's required credit. Unchanged data doesn't trigger a redeploy; ambiguous registrations fail the build.

standard: I built a rune-guessing game and gave Gemini the wolf. It still has to work out the answer.
evidence: You race the wolf to identify a hidden rune. Gemini reads your questions and voices both characters, while the game engine keeps the answer secret and checks every guess. Giving the opponent the answer would have made for a pretty short game.

standard: A brain tracker that can point out a pattern and show me where it came from.
evidence: I record short voice entries, and Gemma looks for patterns on the phone. Every pattern cites the entries behind it, the individual model reads stay visible, and the audio is discarded after processing. It doesn't diagnose me.

standard: A plant scavenger hunt for kids, with a lot of work spent making sure poison ivy couldn't win it.
evidence: The photo checks run on the phone, and code decides whether a find counts. None of the 267 toxic test photos passed. Gemma writes the hints at build time; no language model runs in the app.

standard: I gave ChatGPT and Claude a way to write my index cards without handing either one the database.
evidence: Decisions go from the conversation into Supabase through seven specific tools. Zod checks the input before a write, revisions stay in the history, and a failed batch tells me which cards need another try.

standard: If AI helped write the code, the commit should say so.
evidence: I built Node and Python linters to check AI-attribution footers and human sign-off before a commit lands. They can enforce the format. Whether the credit is honest still takes a person reading it.

standard: I followed the electricity back to the coal mines and their safety records.
evidence: Unearthed connects an address to the grid feeding it and lets you ask questions about the data. Cortex Analyst writes the SQL; I restrict it to one read-only statement, a 10-second timeout, and 500 rows. An interesting question doesn't need an unlimited warehouse bill.

standard: My path from a coal-mining town to software, told as an interactive memoir.
evidence: I built a scene engine to keep Canvas effects, captions, and audio in step. You can mute it or turn off the shaders and still read the whole story. Screen readers get the DOM; they don't have to make sense of the canvas.
